paragraphs: A hierarchical model represents relationships at multiple levels, but deciding how those levels connect can itself be uncertain. This paper introduces Dynamic Hierarchical Markov Random Fields to handle that uncertainty while predicting class labels from observations. The contribution is a discriminative treatment of structure: the model uses the observed data to assess both the hierarchy and its labels.

The framework separates a structure model from a class label model, expressing both through exponential family distributions. This makes the arrangement of the hierarchy an explicit part of the learning problem. Conditioned on observations, the framework also relaxes independence assumptions made by directed models, allowing a less restrictive account of dependencies.

Exact inference is intractable, so the authors develop a variational approximation for learning parameters and finding a maximum a posteriori structure and label assignment. They apply it to extracting product items offered for sale on web pages. The reported results are promising, supporting the potential usefulness of jointly reasoning about structure and labels in this extraction task.
icml-2007-dynamic-hierarchical-markov-ra.tldr: Dynamic Hierarchical Markov Random Fields jointly infer uncertain hierarchies and labels, with promising results for extracting products from web pages.

paragraphs: Multiple kernel learning lets a model learn a weighted combination of kernels, each providing a way to compare examples. Sparse combination weights can also select which kernels contribute. This paper extends that idea to joint feature maps, which represent inputs together with candidate outputs, providing a principled formulation for classification with multiple classes.

Using a joint representation makes the output side part of kernel learning as well. The method can therefore learn kernels on output spaces, expanding what the learned similarities describe. The authors also establish equivalences among several primal optimization formulations, including formulations with different regularizers, connecting alternative mathematical descriptions of the learning problem.

The paper presents several optimization methods and compares a convex quadratically constrained quadratic program with two semi-infinite linear programs. On toy data, the linear-program formulations run faster than the quadratic-program formulation. Applications of a semi-infinite linear program to three real-world datasets further demonstrate the method's utility. These findings support both the multiclass formulation and the practical value of its alternative optimization routes.
icml-2007-multiclass-multiple-kernel-lea.tldr: Joint feature maps extend multiple kernel learning to multiclass prediction and output-space kernels, with efficient linear-program optimization demonstrated experimentally.

paragraphs: Multi-instance learning provides labels for bags of examples while leaving the individual examples unlabeled. Semi-supervised learning instead combines a small collection of labeled examples with many unlabeled ones. Both settings involve incomplete information about individual labels, but their training data are organized differently. This paper establishes a formal connection between them.

The central result shows that multi-instance learning can be viewed as a special case of semi-supervised learning. This perspective makes methods from one branch available for addressing problems in the other. Building on the connection, the authors introduce MissSVM, which uses a specially constructed semi-supervised support vector machine to solve multi-instance learning problems.

Experiments show that this approach is feasible and that MissSVM is competitive with state-of-the-art multi-instance algorithms. The evidence supports the usefulness of the connection as an algorithm-design principle, beyond its conceptual interest. The reported finding is competitiveness, rather than a claim that the semi-supervised formulation always improves on methods designed directly for labeled bags.
icml-2007-on-the-relation-between-multi-.tldr: The paper casts multi-instance learning as a special case of semi-supervised learning and develops the competitive MissSVM algorithm from that connection.

paragraphs: The same objects can have several useful representations. Web pages, for example, can be connected through hyperlinks or compared through their words. When each representation becomes a graph, combining them raises a modeling question: what shared clustering objective should the combined graph represent? Simply averaging graph weights or Laplacians does not, by itself, explain that objective.

This paper develops multiview spectral clustering by extending normalized cut from one graph to several. Normalized cut supplies a criterion for dividing a graph into groups, so its extension gives the combination of views an explicit organizing principle. The resulting framework has an interpretation as a mixture of Markov chains, with a chain defined on each graph.

The authors then build multiview transductive inference on the clustering framework, using the multiple representations for classification of the data under consideration. Experiments on real-world web classification produce promising results. The contribution is therefore both a principled basis for combining graph views and evidence that the resulting approach can be useful for web classification.
icml-2007-spectral-clustering-and-transd.tldr: Extending normalized cut to multiple graphs gives a principled multiview clustering and transductive learning framework with promising web-classification results.

paragraphs: Transductive learning incorporates unlabeled examples into the learning problem by considering their possible labels. With structured outputs, such as label sequences, each example can have many candidate assignments. Searching across combinations of those assignments creates a combinatorial optimization problem. This paper studies how to make transductive kernel machines workable in that setting.

The authors transform the original nonconvex, constrained problems, which contain discrete choices, into continuous optimization problems without constraints. The discrete optimization parameters are eliminated, and the resulting objectives are differentiable. This reformulation changes how the search can be performed: it permits efficient continuous optimization instead of directly handling the original discrete label-assignment variables.

The resulting generalized transductive support vector machine is evaluated empirically on multiclass classification and label-sequence learning. These applications examine the approach across both class selection and structured prediction. The abstract identifies efficient optimization as a central benefit of the reformulation; it does not claim that differentiability makes the problem convex or guarantees a globally optimal solution.
icml-2007-transductive-support-vector-ma.tldr: The paper reformulates transductive learning for structured outputs as differentiable, unconstrained optimization and evaluates a generalized transductive SVM.

paragraphs: Scientists often assess the same parameterized model using several experiments or datasets. Combining those sources can identify plausible parameter regions more informatively than examining each source alone. The paper considers combinations expressed as weighted sums, where finding a desired level set of the combined function represents the task of locating a scientifically relevant parameter region.

The proposed active learning algorithm chooses two things at every step: a parameter setting and the type of experiment to evaluate there. These choices determine both where new information is gathered and which component of the combined function supplies it. This makes experimental selection part of the search for the desired region, rather than treating the available measurements as fixed.

Tests use synthetic functions and real data for a cosmological model with eight parameters. In those evaluations, the algorithm significantly reduces the number of samples needed to identify the desired regions. The stated benefit concerns sample efficiency in locating level sets, connecting the learning strategy directly to the scientific task of constraining plausible model parameters.
icml-2008-actively-learning-level-sets-o.tldr: An active learning algorithm jointly chooses parameter settings and experiment types to identify desired parameter regions with fewer samples in the reported tests.

paragraphs: This paper examines how supervised learning methods perform when examples have many input dimensions. Its focus is comparative: the authors ask whether the relative strengths of learning algorithms change as dimensionality increases. That question matters because a method that performs well with relatively few input dimensions may occupy a different position when the representation becomes much larger.

The evaluation uses three measures: accuracy, AUC, and squared loss. These provide different perspectives on prediction quality, so the comparison is not organized around a single performance score. The study also explicitly investigates increasing dimensionality, connecting changes in algorithm performance to the size of the input representation.

For relatively low-dimensional problems, the findings agree with earlier studies. At higher dimensions, however, the relative performance of the methods appears to shift. Random forests and neural networks seem best able to learn from the high-dimensional data examined. This is an empirical finding about the study's comparisons, providing evidence that conclusions drawn from lower-dimensional evaluations may not carry over unchanged.
icml-2008-an-empirical-evaluation-of-sup.tldr: The evaluation suggests that algorithm rankings change with dimensionality, with random forests and neural networks appearing strongest on the high-dimensional data studied.

paragraphs: Lasso fits a linear regression model while encouraging some coefficients to become zero, thereby selecting variables. This paper studies when that selection recovers the correct model as the sample size grows. Its analysis considers different rates at which the regularization parameter decreases and characterizes the corresponding probabilities of correct variable selection.

At one particular rate, Lasso includes every variable that belongs in the model with probability approaching one exponentially fast. Yet variables that do not belong still have strictly positive selection probabilities. This combination motivates Bolasso: run Lasso on multiple bootstrap replications of the sample, then retain only variables selected in every replication.

The authors show that intersecting these selected sets leads to consistent model selection through the property established in their analysis. The claim concerns the asymptotic behavior supported by that analysis, rather than perfect selection from every finite sample. Experiments on synthetic data and datasets from the UCI repository compare Bolasso favorably with other linear regression methods, adding empirical support to the theoretical motivation.
icml-2008-bolasso-model-consistent-lasso.tldr: Bolasso intersects variables selected by bootstrap Lasso fits, using an asymptotic selection property to obtain consistent model selection.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor retrieval finds stored examples that are most similar to a query under a chosen dissimilarity measure. Many search structures are designed for metrics, but useful measures need not satisfy metric properties. This paper addresses Bregman divergences, a family that includes KL divergence, Mahalanobis distance, and Itakura–Saito divergence.

The proposed data structure follows the broad organization of a metric ball tree. Its key change is mathematical: it uses convexity properties of Bregman divergences where metric methods rely on the triangle inequality. That substitution is central because Bregman divergences are not metrics in general, so the usual geometric justification for metric search cannot simply be assumed.

Experiments demonstrate speedups over brute-force search reaching several orders of magnitude. These results show that efficient retrieval can be achieved for the tested divergences without evaluating every candidate in the same way as exhaustive search. More broadly, the work identifies a useful route for adapting a familiar search structure to dissimilarities whose mathematical properties differ from ordinary metric distances.
icml-2008-fast-nearest-neighbor-retrieva.tldr: A ball-tree-style structure uses Bregman convexity instead of the triangle inequality, achieving large experimental speedups over brute-force nearest-neighbor search.

paragraphs: This paper uses programmable graphics processors to accelerate support vector machines. It addresses both training, which constructs the classifier, and classification, which applies it to examples. The motivation is the substantial parallel computing capacity of GPUs, which creates opportunities for faster implementations of machine learning algorithms.

For training, the authors implement a solver based on Platt's Sequential Minimal Optimization algorithm. It uses an adaptive working-set selection heuristic incorporating first- and second-order information. Working-set selection determines which parts of the optimization problem receive attention during an update. The reported training implementation runs 9–35 times faster than LIBSVM on a conventional processor.

The paper also presents a GPU classification system. It achieves reported speedups of 81–138 times over LIBSVM and 5–24 times over the authors' own CPU classifier. Those separate comparisons matter because the observed gain depends on the CPU implementation used as the reference. Together, the results demonstrate substantial acceleration for both stages of SVM use in the reported evaluations.
icml-2008-fast-support-vector-machine-tr.tldr: GPU implementations accelerate SVM training by 9–35 times and classification by 81–138 times relative to LIBSVM in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Gaussian process regression often assumes stationarity, but the scale of variation in data may change across the input space. Explicitly designing a nonstationary covariance function can require detailed prior knowledge of those changes. This paper proposes a Gaussian process product model that learns nonstationary amplitude variation through a flexible latent representation.

The model represents the data as the pointwise product of two hidden Gaussian processes. Their outputs are multiplied at corresponding inputs, allowing the amplitude behavior to be inferred through the latent functions. The approach operates on outputs rather than inputs. The authors report that this reduces computation and data requirements relative to other nonparametric covariance-inference approaches while improving scalability to high-dimensional inputs.

Inference uses an approximate scheme based on Expectation Propagation. The resulting variational approximation supports convenient selection of Gaussian process hyperparameters and compact approximate predictive distributions. The contribution combines a representation for changing amplitude with a practical inference method, addressing both how nonstationarity is modeled and how predictions can be obtained from that model.
icml-2008-gaussian-process-product-model.tldr: Multiplying two latent Gaussian processes provides a nonparametric model of changing amplitude, with approximate inference designed to reduce computational and data demands.

paragraphs: Point clouds describe objects as sets of points in two or three dimensions. Learning from them requires comparisons that respect relevant geometric invariances and practical constraints. This paper extends graph kernels to point clouds, enabling kernel methods to work with representations such as shapes, line drawings, and three-dimensional collections of points.

The authors construct these comparisons using kernels between covariance matrices and factorizations of those matrices on graphical models. Their design aims to combine expressive comparisons with numerical efficiency and relatively few free parameters. This connects the geometric representation of an object to a structured calculation of similarity, rather than treating a point set as an unstructured collection.

The paper derives dynamic programming recursions that compute the proposed quantities in polynomial time. Applications involve recognizing handwritten digits and Chinese characters using few training examples. These applications demonstrate how the point-cloud kernels can support recognition tasks, while the computational development addresses the practical challenge of evaluating rich similarities between geometric objects.
icml-2008-graph-kernels-between-point-cl.tldr: The paper extends graph kernels to geometric point clouds and derives polynomial-time computations, with applications to recognition from few examples.

paragraphs: Image segmentation groups parts of an image into regions. This paper applies a kernel stick-breaking process to small pixel patches, making nearby patches more likely to share a segment. Spatial proximity therefore influences the grouping probabilistically. The hierarchical Bayesian model also infers the number of segments, so that number does not have to be fixed beforehand.

The authors extend the approach to multiple images by combining the kernel stick-breaking process with a shared Dirichlet process prior. This allows the images to be modeled together while their interrelationships are inferred. The shared model connects segmentation with a broader image-analysis goal: learning how different images relate to one another.

Inference combines variational Bayesian analysis with local sampling. The paper describes this computational framework and presents example results for several image-analysis problems. The authors suggest that the multiple-image formulation may be useful for sorting images and learning their relationships. That proposed usefulness follows from the model's ability to share information across images, while remaining a qualified application claim.
icml-2008-hierarchical-kernel-stick-brea.tldr: A hierarchical Bayesian model infers image segments and their number, while a shared prior enables joint modeling of relationships across images.

paragraphs: A decision-making problem can have several reward criteria, with different preferences assigning different importance to each. This paper develops an algorithm that learns optimal policies across linear combinations of those criteria. Its target is a solution that supports any linear preference assignment, rather than requiring the entire problem to be expressed through one fixed weighting.

The algorithm extends the backup operation used in reinforcement learning for Markov decision processes. Instead of retaining only a maximal expected reward for a single objective, it backs up a set of expected reward outcomes. Each retained outcome is maximal for some set of preference weights, preserving alternatives that can matter under different linear preferences.

The authors provide a correctness proof showing that the solution yields an optimal policy for any linear preference function. For a specific weight vector, the approach reduces to standard value iteration. The linear form of the preferences is central to the stated result: the guarantee concerns weighted combinations of the reward criteria, not unrestricted ways of expressing preferences.
icml-2008-learning-all-optimal-policies-.tldr: Set-valued reward backups extend value iteration to recover an optimal policy for any linear weighting of multiple reward criteria.

paragraphs: Demonstrations of a maneuver can contain imperfections even when they come from an expert. This paper studies learning from a small number of such demonstrations when the intended trajectory is initially unknown. The goal is to recover the desired movement and learn enough about the system to control it along that movement.

The proposed algorithm performs both tasks: it extracts a desired trajectory from the demonstrations and learns a local model suitable for control along that trajectory. This separates the intended behavior from imperfections in its demonstrated execution. The local model then supplies the control-relevant description associated with the recovered trajectory.

Applied to autonomous helicopter flight, the system exceeds the expert pilot's demonstrated performance in every reported case. The authors report first autonomous executions of tic-tocs, loops, and a hurricane, as well as substantially improved flips and rolls. They also demonstrate a complete airshow requiring autonomous transitions between maneuvers. These results show that, in the reported helicopter tasks, learning from suboptimal demonstrations can support performance beyond those demonstrations.
icml-2008-learning-for-control-from-mult.tldr: Learning an intended trajectory and local control model from imperfect demonstrations enables autonomous helicopter aerobatics that outperform the demonstrated flights.

paragraphs: This paper presents a system that learns to commentate on simulated soccer games from human commentary and game states. Its training information is ambiguous: the system must determine how pieces of language correspond to what is happening in the simulation. It learns both to interpret and to generate commentary without engineered knowledge of English.

The learning process jointly establishes correspondences between commentary and simulation states and constructs a translation model. These two tasks are connected because identifying what an utterance describes helps explain its language, while learning the language helps identify the relevant state. The system therefore learns the relationship between words and the events they describe from the supplied paired sources.

Generating commentary also requires choosing which events deserve mention. The authors introduce Iterative Generation Strategy Learning to address that selection problem. Human evaluations judge the generated commentaries to be of reasonable quality relative to human commentaries. The result supports the feasibility of learning both language use and event selection from ambiguous supervision in this simulated-soccer setting.
icml-2008-learning-to-sportscast-a-test-.tldr: A simulated-soccer commentator learns language grounding and event selection from ambiguous supervision, producing commentary judged reasonably good by human evaluators.

paragraphs: The paper addresses classification across a large number of related tasks, motivated by predicting HIV therapy outcomes. A prediction depends on observed genetic properties of a patient's virus and the drug combination being considered. Hundreds of combinations create many prediction tasks, and some combinations have few or no training examples of their own.

The proposed solution produces resampling weights that make the pooled examples match the target distribution of a given task. This allows data collected across tasks to contribute according to their relevance to the particular prediction problem. The application also contains relationships between therapies, since some drug combinations act through similar biochemical mechanisms.

The authors report that multi-task learning enables predictions for combinations with little or no direct training data and substantially improves overall prediction accuracy. The important connection is between sharing examples and adapting that shared pool to each target task. The reported outcome concerns predictive performance in therapy screening, showing how related tasks can provide useful information when individual combinations are sparsely represented.
icml-2008-multi-task-learning-for-hiv-th.tldr: Task-specific resampling of pooled data improves HIV therapy outcome prediction and supports drug combinations with few or no training examples.

paragraphs: Multiple instance ranking addresses situations where groups must be ordered even though the responsible individual within a group is unknown. The paper motivates this problem through hydrogen abstraction during metabolism. The goal is to predict which grouping of hydrogen atoms in a molecule is preferred, while the particular hydrogen removed within that grouping remains ambiguous.

The proposed MIRank model represents the task as ranking groups in a multiple-instance setting. This matches the requested prediction to the available supervision: the model learns which group should be preferred without requiring identification of the specific member responsible. The paper formulates the problem generally, extending its relevance beyond the motivating chemistry application.

The authors propose an algorithm based on successive linear programming to solve MIRank problems. On several real and synthetic datasets, the method outperforms multiple-instance classification models. Those results support treating relative preference as an explicit learning objective when the desired output is an ordering of groups and the underlying instance-level explanation is uncertain.
icml-2008-multiple-instance-ranking-d80f.tldr: MIRank learns to rank groups despite uncertainty about their individual members, outperforming multiple-instance classification models on the reported datasets.

paragraphs: In high-dimensional classification, training examples cannot densely cover every class region. Gaps and irregularities in the samples can produce irregular decision boundaries for local methods. This paper models each class as a convex region and classifies new examples through their distances to those approximate regions, providing a way to fill gaps in the observed samples.

The proposed class model is a bounding hyperdisk: the intersection of the samples' affine hull and their smallest enclosing hypersphere. The authors argue that this gives tighter bounds than either an affine hull or a hypersphere alone. They also argue that it avoids much of the overfitting and computational complexity associated with high-dimensional convex hulls.

The hyperdisk method can be kernelized, allowing nonlinear classifiers based on non-Euclidean distance metrics. Experiments on several classification problems yield promising results. The geometric argument is qualified: hyperdisks are presented as preferable in many cases, rather than universally best. Their appeal lies in balancing how tightly a class is represented against sensitivity to sparse samples and computational demands.
icml-2008-nearest-hyperdisk-methods-for-.tldr: Bounding hyperdisks offer compact class-region models for sparse high-dimensional data, with kernelized extensions and promising classification results.

paragraphs: Nonnegative matrix factorization approximates a nonnegative data matrix using two smaller nonnegative factors. This paper proposes rank-one downdate, or R1D, as a way to compute such a factorization. The method is partly inspired by singular value decomposition and builds its representation through components extracted from adaptively chosen portions of the data.

At each iteration, R1D extracts a rank-one submatrix according to an objective function. It computes dominant singular values and vectors of the selected submatrices, connecting the iterative extraction procedure to established matrix decomposition ideas. The adaptive choice of submatrices determines which portion of the dataset contributes to the component being identified.

The authors establish that maximizing their objective corresponds to correctly classifying articles when the corpus is nearly separable. That condition is part of the theoretical result. Computational experiments also show successful feature identification in realistic datasets, and the paper reports that the method is much faster than LSI and other NMF routines. Together, these contributions connect the extraction objective to a conditional guarantee and practical computational results.
icml-2008-nonnegative-matrix-factorizati.tldr: R1D computes nonnegative factorizations through adaptive rank-one extraction, with a nearly separable-corpus guarantee and strong reported computational performance.

paragraphs: Predicting which genes are essential helps investigate the minimal requirements for life and informs work on cellular mechanisms and therapeutic drugs. This paper develops kernel-based approaches to predicting essentiality from protein sequences. The authors report solutions that outperform existing models while using less training data, making sequence comparison central to the prediction task.

The first approach uses a partly hand-designed kernel derived from several domains in the Pfam database. The paper then introduces general domain-based sequence kernels that compare sequences with respect to domains containing large collections of protein sequences. This replaces the semi-manual construction with a broader mechanism for expressing domain-related sequence similarity.

Computing these kernels presents a scale challenge: there can be thousands of domains, with thousands of sequences in some individual domains. The authors use automata to represent and efficiently compute the kernels. Extensive experiments show that the general kernels compare favorably with the Pfam kernel for essentiality prediction while requiring no manual tuning, linking computational tractability with useful predictive performance.
icml-2008-sequence-kernels-for-predictin.tldr: Domain-based sequence kernels use automata for efficient protein-essentiality prediction and compare favorably with a semi-manual Pfam kernel without manual tuning.

paragraphs: The paper studies linear regression when the number of unknown coefficients greatly exceeds the number of observations. The observations are modeled as a known design matrix multiplied by a coefficient vector, plus random error. The estimation target is the mean response represented by that matrix-vector product, with particular attention to sparse coefficient estimates.

The authors propose flexible Bayesian models that can yield such sparse estimates. Sparsity means that the fitted representation can rely on a limited subset of the available coefficients, even though the parameter vector is large. This directly addresses the structure of the problem under study: many possible contributions must be considered from a much smaller observation vector.

The paper also examines what happens as the number of coefficients tends to infinity, establishing a close relationship between the proposed models and a class of Lévy processes. Simulations show significant improvements over a range of popular alternatives. The contribution thus combines a flexible sparse-regression construction, an infinite-dimensional mathematical connection, and empirical evidence from simulated problems.
icml-2008-sparse-bayesian-nonparametric-.tldr: Flexible Bayesian regression models produce sparse estimates, connect to Lévy processes in an infinite-dimensional limit, and outperform alternatives in simulations.

paragraphs: Clustering with advice supplements the data with guidance about how groups should be formed. Such guidance can be inconsistent, creating a challenge for methods that must reconcile the clustering objective with the supplied advice. This paper brings that problem into spectral clustering, where the authors identify a gap between earlier theoretical work on inconsistency and existing clustering methods.

The proposed framework seeks minimum normalized cuts subject to inconsistent advice. Normalized cut supplies the graph-partitioning objective, while the advice adds information about the desired grouping. Bringing both into one framework makes inconsistency part of the clustering problem being addressed. The work extends an existing approach by De Bie and Cristianini.

The authors' results suggest that the framework can succeed in many situations. That is a qualified assessment of its promise, rather than a universal guarantee for every collection of conflicting advice. The contribution is the explicit incorporation of inconsistent guidance into a normalized-cut framework, broadening the kinds of supervision that spectral clustering can attempt to accommodate.
icml-2008-spectral-clustering-with-incon.tldr: The paper extends normalized-cut spectral clustering to incorporate inconsistent advice, with results suggesting usefulness across many situations.

paragraphs: Evaluating an agent through repeated play can require many samples when both its decisions and the game's outcomes are stochastic. Ordinary Monte Carlo estimates may fluctuate substantially, making accurate comparisons expensive. This paper addresses that problem for extensive games, where evaluation must account for the unfolding sequence of decisions and outcomes.

The proposed technique evaluates many strategies simultaneously while only one strategy is played. It uses importance sampling to make the observations useful for evaluating those different strategies. The paper adds two mechanisms that significantly reduce the variance of the estimates, addressing the instability that makes straightforward sampling inefficient.

The authors demonstrate the technique in poker, a domain where stochasticity makes conventional evaluation problematic. The finding supports the practical value of sharing sampled experience across strategy evaluations while reducing estimation noise. Its significance is an improvement in how strategies can be assessed: collecting experience under one played strategy can inform several evaluations, and lower-variance estimates can make that information more useful.
icml-2008-strategy-evaluation-in-extensi.tldr: An importance-sampling technique evaluates multiple strategies from play under one strategy, using two variance-reduction mechanisms demonstrated in poker.

paragraphs: Similarity matrices from applications do not always satisfy the positive-semidefinite requirement of the standard kernel-machine framework. This paper studies how to train support vector machines when the supplied kernel matrix is indefinite. Its approach treats that matrix as a noisy observation of an unknown positive-semidefinite proxy that can be learned.

The regularized formulation computes the proxy kernel and support vectors together, connecting the adjustment of similarities to the classifier being trained. The authors express the optimization as a semi-infinite quadratically constrained linear program and provide an iterative solution method that reaches a global optimum. This gives a principled optimization route for the proposed formulation.

An additional pruning strategy substantially improves efficiency while preserving the algorithm's convergence property. The paper also establishes a close relationship with multiple kernel learning, connecting the proxy-kernel approach to another framework for learning similarities. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate efficiency and effectiveness, supporting the practical use of the joint formulation when the original similarity matrix is indefinite.
icml-2008-training-svm-with-indefinite-k.tldr: A regularized SVM jointly learns a positive-semidefinite proxy for an indefinite kernel and its support vectors through globally solvable optimization.
